items.prompt: In the debt metaphor, what is the principal?
choices: The cost of building it the proper way
The bugs the shortcut causes later
The time that the shortcut saved up front
items.explanation: Principal is the cost of the proper version. The bugs and friction are the interest.

items.prompt: In the debt metaphor, what is the interest?
choices: The extra cost paid each sprint it stays
The salary of the engineer who took it
The upfront cost of building the proper version
items.explanation: Interest recurs every sprint: workarounds, bugs, rework.

items.prompt: Which attitude treats debt as a trade-off?
choices: Refusing every shortcut under any deadline
Calling every messy file debt on sight
Borrowing on purpose and planning to repay
items.explanation: The metaphor is a financial choice, not a moral failing.

items.prompt: Code was written carelessly with no deadline and gained nothing. Is it debt?
choices: No, it is just low quality
Yes, all unclean code is debt
Yes, but only once it is old
items.explanation: Debt implies you got something for it, such as speed. With nothing gained there is no loan.

items.prompt: What does a default look like for technical debt?
choices: Repaid a sprint late
Never repaid, so velocity collapses
The principal was estimated slightly high
items.explanation: Default means interest keeps compounding until the team can barely move.

items.prompt: Who coined the technical debt metaphor?
choices: Grace Hopper
Ward Cunningham
Margaret Hamilton
items.explanation: Cunningham used it to describe borrowing to ship sooner. Fowler later added the quadrant.

items.prompt: A team refuses every shortcut despite a real deadline. What does it ignore?
choices: That the deadline could be moved later
That interest never applies to debt
That borrowing can be the right call
items.explanation: Treating all debt as sin is one of the two opposite mistakes.

items.prompt: What do you receive in exchange for taking on debt?
choices: Speed or a market window to hit
A lower cost on every later task
Permission to skip repaying it
items.explanation: A nameable benefit on the other side is what makes it a loan.

items.prompt: Lumeo ships a single-customer data layer in 2 days instead of 15. Which pairing is right?
choices: The proper build is the principal; friction is the interest
The 2 days saved is the principal; the 15 days is the interest
Sprint friction is the principal; the deadline is the interest
The 13 days saved is the interest; the contract is the principal
items.explanation: The proper build is the principal; the recurring friction of keeping the shortcut is the interest.
items.reference:
The loan, mapped to code
principal: cost of the proper version, paid whenever
interest: extra cost every sprint the shortcut stays
default: never repaid, velocity collapses
no benefit gained: not a loan, just low quality
Why: debt is a trade-off with a nameable benefit and a payback plan, not a synonym for bad code.
items.learnMore:
Debt as a loan

Cunningham's metaphor treats a shortcut like borrowed money: you get speed now, and pay interest until you repay the principal. The point is to count the cost, not to ban borrowing.

Common mistake

Using the word for any messy code. If nothing was gained, there is no loan to name.
items.reflection: Think of something you put off on purpose, like a repair or a document. What was the principal, what was the interest, and did you pick a payback date?

items.prompt: A module was sloppy when written, saved no time, and no deadline pushed it. Why is calling it debt misleading?
choices: Debt only applies to modules more than a year old
Nothing was gained, so there is no loan to point to
Sloppy modules always carry a lower interest rate
Debt only applies to code that compiles with warnings
items.explanation: A real debt has a nameable benefit on the other side. Without one, it is plain low quality.

items.prompt: In the quadrant, what does deliberate mean?
choices: The shortcut was cheap
The shortcut was chosen knowingly
The shortcut was reviewed by two people
items.explanation: Deliberate versus inadvertent asks whether the choice was made on purpose.

items.prompt: In the quadrant, what does prudent mean?
choices: Taken without weighing the cost at all
A reasonable bet given what was known
Taken by the most experienced person here
items.explanation: Prudent versus reckless asks whether the decision was reasoned.

items.prompt: Which box is the acceptable trade-off?
choices: Inadvertent
Deliberate and prudent
Deliberate and reckless
items.explanation: Only a chosen, reasoned shortcut with a plan counts as acceptable.

items.prompt: A team never knew a cost was being incurred. Which is it?
choices: Inadvertent
Deliberate
Prudent by definition
items.explanation: Not knowing a cost existed means no decision was ever made.

items.prompt: 'We know, and we have a plan' fits which box?
choices: Deliberate and prudent
Inadvertent and reckless
Inadvertent
items.explanation: A plan is what makes a deliberate shortcut prudent.

items.prompt: 'We do not have time for the right way' with no plan fits which box?
choices: Deliberate and prudent
Deliberate and reckless
Inadvertent and prudent
items.explanation: Chosen on purpose, but with no plan to repay.

items.prompt: The team later learns a better design. Which box is this?
choices: Deliberate and reckless
Inadvertent and reckless
Inadvertent and prudent
items.explanation: They did their best with what they knew, then learned more.

items.prompt: Does the same code always sit in the same box?
choices: Yes, the code itself decides the box
Yes, the language used decides the box
No, the decision around it decides
items.explanation: The quadrant describes the decision-making, not the code itself.

items.prompt: Two engineers write identical single-customer code. One chose it for a deadline and logged a repay date; the other never knew multi-customer was needed. What separates them?
choices: The decision around the code, not the code
The first one used fewer lines of code overall
The second one has a larger principal to repay
The first one is written in a faster language
items.explanation: The quadrant classifies the decision: deliberate and prudent versus inadvertent.
items.reference:
The quadrant
deliberate + prudent: we know, and we have a plan
deliberate + reckless: no time for the right way
inadvertent + prudent: now we know a better way
inadvertent + reckless: what is tenant isolation?
Why: two independent questions, chosen or not and reasoned or not, give four different situations.
items.learnMore:
Four kinds of debt

Crossing deliberate/inadvertent with prudent/reckless splits one pile called tech debt into four. The same code can sit in different boxes depending on whether anyone weighed the cost and planned repayment.

Common mistake

Treating the box as a property of the code. It describes the decision made around it.
items.reflection: Recall a past decision you now regret. Which box did it sit in when you made it, and which box would you say it was in once you understood more?

items.prompt: Nadia took a shortcut for a real deadline but told nobody and left no note. Which box is it now?
choices: Deliberate and prudent, since the reason was real
Deliberate but reckless, since no plan exists
Inadvertent and prudent, since no one noticed it
Inadvertent and reckless, since she did not choose it
items.explanation: Without visibility or a plan, a deliberate choice is indistinguishable from an unweighed one.

items.prompt: Nadia's principal is $9,000 and interest $1,200 a sprint. What is the break-even in sprints?
items.explanation: 9,000 divided by 1,200 is 7.5 sprints.

items.prompt: What happens to cumulative interest each sprint the shortcut stays?
choices: It stays the same as the sprint before
It grows by one more sprint of interest
It falls by the amount of the principal
items.explanation: Cumulative interest rises by $1,200 each sprint in the model.

items.prompt: In the simple model, what does the principal line do over time?
choices: It rises steadily each sprint
It stays flat at $9,000
It shrinks a little
items.explanation: The model holds principal at $9,000, the cost of the proper build.

items.prompt: When cumulative interest passes the principal, what is true?
choices: The shortcut becomes free to carry
Carrying it now costs more than fixing it
The principal doubles to cover the interest
items.explanation: Past the crossing, each sprint of waiting costs more than the fix would have.

items.prompt: Interest of $1,200 a sprint, how much is paid after 4 sprints?
Which two numbers do you compare to size a shortcut?
choices: Lines of code and number of tests
Principal and interest per sprint
Team size and the length of a sprint
items.explanation: Those are the two terms of any loan.

items.prompt: Why compare projected interest, not today's interest?
choices: Interest keeps growing until repayment
Today's interest is zero
Principal changes every day in practice
items.explanation: Today's interest is small on day one of every loan.

items.prompt: Is the principal always fixed in real projects?
choices: No, it can grow as more code depends on it
Yes, it is fixed once the shortcut is taken
Yes, but it can change inside one sprint
items.explanation: More code on the shortcut means a wider retrofit later.

items.prompt: Principal is $9,000, interest $1,200 a sprint. In which whole sprint does cumulative interest first exceed the principal?
choices: The 8th, at $9,600
The 7th, at $8,400
The 9th, at $10,800
The 6th, at $7,200
items.explanation: Break-even is 7.5, so after 7 sprints it is $8,400 (below) and after 8 it is $9,600 (above).
items.reference:
Interest vs. principal
principal: $9,000 (15 days at $600, assumed)
interest: $1,200 per sprint
break-even: 9,000 / 1,200 = 7.5 sprints
sprint 8: $9,600 paid, already past the fix
Why: carrying a shortcut is cheap until accumulated interest meets the cost of the proper fix.
items.learnMore:
Sizing a shortcut

Compare principal to the interest you will have paid by the planned repayment date. Divide principal by interest per sprint for a break-even. The numbers are estimates, so the value is in naming both.

Common mistake

Comparing today's interest to today's principal. That is true on day one of every loan.
items.reflection: Pick a recurring annoyance you tolerate, like a slow manual step. What does it cost per week, and what would fixing it cost once? When do they cross?

It treats the principal as larger than it is

items.prompt: What is a debt log?
choices: A running list of every bug the team has ever fixed
A private note one engineer keeps
A shared record of shortcuts and payback dates
items.explanation: It makes the trade-off visible to the whole team.

items.prompt: Name one thing a good debt entry records.
choices: Why the shortcut was taken
The yearly salary
The text editor that was used
items.explanation: The reason lets later readers tell temporary from permanent.

items.prompt: Why does a log help when someone changes teams?
choices: It deletes the shortcut as soon as they leave
The knowledge is not stuck in one memory
It raises the principal of the debt
items.explanation: A row in a shared log outlives any one person's memory.

items.prompt: What does a log row put in front of planning?
choices: A hidden risk
A number that competes for priority
A finished feature ready to be shipped
items.explanation: Without a number, repayment loses to whatever is louder.

items.prompt: Who should be able to read the debt log?
choices: Only the author
Only managers
The whole team
items.explanation: Visibility is the point.

items.prompt: A repay-by sprint is written in the log. Is repayment now guaranteed?
choices: Yes, automatically
Yes, once a reviewer has approved the row
No, planning still has to protect it
items.explanation: A date only helps if planning acts on it.

items.prompt: Debt known only to one engineer is usually repaid how?
choices: On schedule
By accident, if at all
By the compiler, which flags old code
items.explanation: Nothing forces anyone to revisit it.

items.prompt: A shortcut bought nothing. Should it go in the debt log?
choices: Yes, always
Yes, with a low priority
No, just fix it
items.explanation: A real debt has a nameable benefit. Without one, it is low quality.

items.prompt: DEBT-001 was logged at sprint 1, but four new features since then assume one customer. What is the biggest risk?
choices: The real principal has grown beyond the logged $9,000
The interest per sprint has now dropped to exactly zero
The debt has silently moved into the inadvertent box
The log entry has itself become the source of the debt
items.explanation: More code on the shortcut widens the retrofit, so a log that never re-estimates understates urgency.
items.reference:
What makes debt visible
a shared row: id, reason, principal, interest, repay-by, owner
read at planning, not only at launch
principal re-estimated as more code depends on it
no benefit gained: do not log it, fix it
Why: a shortcut counts as deliberate and prudent only if others can see it and act on it.
items.learnMore:
Making debt visible

A log survives people changing teams, puts a number in front of planning, and tells later readers why code looks the way it does. It has to be read and its figures refreshed to keep working.

Common mistake

Writing the row once and archiving it. Interest and principal keep changing.
items.reflection: Think of a promise you made informally, to a colleague or friend. Where was it written down, and what happened to it when you were busy?

Reasons expire after one sprint of use
items.explanation: To later readers, an unrecorded choice looks the same as no choice at all.

items.prompt: Implement `cumulativeInterest(perSprint, sprints)`: the total interest paid after that many sprints.
items.explanation: Interest is flat, so the total is the per-sprint amount times the number of sprints.

items.prompt: Implement `stillCheaperToCarry(principal, perSprint, sprints)`: true while interest paid is strictly below the principal.
items.explanation: Compare accumulated interest to the principal. Past the crossing, carrying costs more than fixing.

items.prompt: Implement `loadedCost(days, dayRate)`: the principal for a fix that takes that many engineer-days.
items.explanation: Principal is days of work times the loaded daily rate.

items.prompt: Implement `overPrincipal(principal, perSprint, sprints)`: how many dollars the interest paid exceeds the principal, or 0 if it has not yet.
items.explanation: Subtract the principal from accumulated interest, and clamp at zero before the crossing.

items.prompt: Implement `breakEvenSprint(principal, perSprint)`: the first whole sprint in which cumulative interest reaches or exceeds the principal. Assume both are positive.
items.explanation: Divide principal by interest and round up, because repayment happens on whole sprints. An exact multiple (9,000 / 1,500 = 6) hits break-even on that sprint, so ceil keeps it at 6.
items.reference:
Break-even arithmetic
interest paid = per-sprint interest x sprints
break-even = principal / interest per sprint
first whole sprint past it = round the break-even up
9,000 / 1,200 = 7.5, so the 8th sprint
Why: the repayment date is the first whole sprint where interest paid reaches the principal.
items.learnMore:
Computing the break-even

Divide principal by interest per sprint, then round up, because repayment happens on a whole sprint. All figures are assumptions the team estimates, so rerun with ranges.

Common mistake

Rounding down. At 7 sprints the interest is still below the principal.
items.reflection: Name a cost you carry that has a one-off fix. Roughly how many weeks until carrying it costs more than fixing it, and would you notice the day it crossed?

items.prompt: Implement `sprintsToRepayBy(principal, perSprint, deadlineSprint)`: how many sprints before `deadlineSprint` the team should repay, i.e. the deadline minus the first whole break-even sprint. Return 0 if the deadline is earlier.
items.explanation: Compute the whole-sprint break-even, then subtract it from the deadline and clamp at zero so an early deadline gives no advance repayment.

Common mistake

Rounding down. At 7 sprints the interest is still below the principal.
